value.overview: The White-fronted Tyrannulet (Acrochordopus zeledoni) is a small, little-known tyrant flycatcher of humid mountain forests in the Neotropics. It is usually encountered high in the forest, where it searches foliage for insects and takes small fruits. The species has a notably fragmented distribution, with separate populations in Central America, the Andes, northern Venezuela, and the tepui region of southern Venezuela. Its quiet, canopy-oriented habits can make it easy to overlook, even where it is locally established.
value.classification: The White-fronted Tyrannulet belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. It is placed in the genus Acrochordopus; older references may use Phyllomyias zeledoni or Pogonotriccus zeledoni.
value.identification: A small, predominantly olive-green and gray tyrannulet with a conspicuous whitish forehead and generally pale facial markings. The upperparts are olive, while the underparts are paler, often with a subdued yellowish or grayish wash. It has a short, pointed bill and a compact flycatcher shape. Identification is often difficult because it moves actively in foliage, stays near the canopy, and may be detected first by its sharp, high-pitched calls rather than by a prolonged view.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-fronted Tyrannulet has a disjunct range extending from Costa Rica and western Panama through several isolated mountain regions of northern and southern Venezuela and along the eastern Andes from Colombia to Peru. In Costa Rica, the nominate subspecies occurs in the mountains, including the Cordillera de Tilarán and other humid highland areas, generally from foothill elevations to about 2,800 meters. It uses humid evergreen forest, forest edges, clearings with scattered trees, and mature secondary woodland, especially in the canopy and upper levels.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. There is no reliable evidence of regular long-distance migration, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or changing conditions.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the White-fronted Tyrannulet remains poorly documented. A nest recorded in Panama was a cup made largely of moss and placed on a horizontal branch in the canopy, about 12 meters above the ground. Both members of the pair reportedly helped construct it. The breeding season has not been fully defined; available observations include nesting activity or breeding evidence in August in Panama. Reliable information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care is limited.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet is incompletely known but includes arthropods and small berries. It usually forages alone or in mixed-species feeding flocks, mainly in the middle and upper forest levels. The bird gleans prey and fruit from foliage and branches, sometimes making short hovering movements to reach items. Its small bill and active behavior are typical of an insect-oriented canopy tyrannulet, but the relative importance of animal and plant food is not well established.
value.behavior: The White-fronted Tyrannulet is an active, canopy-associated bird that is often encountered singly or with mixed feeding flocks. It moves rapidly through foliage and may make brief hovering flights while feeding. Vocal activity is greatest in the morning. Its song or main call has been described as a high, piercing note, sometimes repeated in a series or delivered as a descending sequence of several notes. Because it is local and inconspicuous, it is frequently overlooked during forest surveys.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is believed to be decreasing, although the rate and geographic pattern of decline are uncertain.
